prompt: In chemistry, what is a mole (mol)?

choices.text: A specific number of things: about 6.022 × 10^23 of them
A specific mass of a substance: 12 g of it
choices.why: A mole is a count of things, not a mass, just as a dozen is a count of twelve things.

choices.text: The mass of a single atom or molecule, in grams
choices.why: A single atom or molecule has a tiny mass, far less than a gram. A mole is a number of particles, and a huge one.

choices.text: A specific volume of a substance: 1 L of it
choices.why: A mole is a count of particles, like a dozen, not an amount of space.

explanation: A mole means a specific number of things, just as a dozen means twelve things. The number is very large: 1 mol = 6.022 × 10^23 things, a value called Avogadro's number.

prompt: A mole is often compared to a dozen. In what way are the two units alike?

choices.text: Each stands for a definite number of things.
Each stands for the same number of things, twelve.
choices.why: A dozen is 12, but a mole is 6.022 × 10^23, a vastly larger number.

choices.text: Each is used to count atoms and molecules only.
choices.why: A dozen usually counts everyday things like eggs, and a mole can count anything. Chemists just usually use the mole for atoms and molecules.

choices.text: Each stands for a definite mass of things.
choices.why: Neither unit is a mass. A dozen eggs and a dozen bricks have very different masses, even though both are twelve things.

explanation: A dozen means 12 things and a mole means 6.022 × 10^23 things. Both are counts, so either can count anything: atoms, molecules, or even eggs.

prompt: Why is the mole such an important unit in chemistry?

choices.text: It links a number of particles to a mass in grams.
It lets chemists count atoms one at a time as they react.
choices.why: Samples contain far too many atoms to count one at a time. The mole lets chemists work with huge numbers of them at once.

choices.text: It is the smallest amount of a substance that can react.
choices.why: Single atoms and molecules react with each other. A mole is just a convenient, very large number of them.

choices.text: It is a unit of mass that replaces the gram for tiny samples.
choices.why: A mole is a number of particles, not a mass. Masses are still measured in grams, and the mole links the two.

explanation: We never handle atoms or molecules one at a time; real samples contain enormous numbers of them. The mole counts particles in a convenient unit and, through the molar mass, links that count to grams, connecting the microscopic and the macroscopic.

prompt: Sample A is 1.00 mol of helium atoms, and sample B is 1.00 mol of gold atoms. How do the two samples compare? (Molar masses: He, 4.0026 g/mol; Au, 196.97 g/mol.)

choices.text: They have the same number of atoms, but the gold has far more mass.
They have the same mass, but the helium has far more atoms.
choices.why: Both are 1.00 mol, so both contain 6.022 × 10^23 atoms. Their masses differ: 4.00 g of helium versus 197 g of gold.

choices.text: They have the same number of atoms and the same mass.
choices.why: The numbers of atoms match, but each gold atom is much heavier than a helium atom, so the gold sample has the greater mass.

choices.text: The helium has more atoms, because helium atoms are smaller.
choices.why: The size of the atoms doesn't matter: 1 mol of anything contains 6.022 × 10^23 particles.

explanation: Both samples contain 6.022 × 10^23 atoms, because that is what 1.00 mol means. Their masses differ because the atoms differ: 1.00 mol of helium is 4.00 g, while 1.00 mol of gold is 197 g.

prompt: Sample A is 1.00 mol of hydrogen atoms, H. Sample B is 1.00 mol of hydrogen molecules, H2. How do the numbers of hydrogen atoms in the two samples compare?

choices.text: Sample B has twice as many hydrogen atoms as sample A.
Both samples have the same number of hydrogen atoms.
choices.why: Both contain 6.022 × 10^23 particles, but each particle in sample B is an H2 molecule made of two atoms.

choices.text: Sample A has twice as many hydrogen atoms as sample B.
choices.why: This is reversed. Sample B has as many H2 molecules as sample A has atoms, and each molecule holds two atoms.

choices.text: They can't be compared without knowing the masses.
choices.why: The moles already give the counts: 6.022 × 10^23 atoms in A, and 6.022 × 10^23 molecules, or 1.204 × 10^24 atoms, in B.

explanation: A mole is 6.022 × 10^23 of whatever particle is named. Sample A has 6.022 × 10^23 H atoms; sample B has 6.022 × 10^23 H2 molecules, which contain 2 × 6.022 × 10^23 = 1.204 × 10^24 H atoms.

prompt: What is the molar mass of a substance?

choices.text: The mass, in grams, of 1 mol of the substance
The mass, in grams, of one atom or molecule of it
choices.why: One particle's mass in grams is tiny. Molar mass is the mass of a whole mole, 6.022 × 10^23 particles.

choices.text: The number of moles in 1 g of the substance
choices.why: That is the reciprocal of the molar mass. Molar mass is grams per mole, not moles per gram.

choices.text: The number of particles in 1 mol of the substance
choices.why: That is Avogadro's number, 6.022 × 10^23, which is the same for every substance. Molar mass differs from one substance to another.

explanation: Molar mass is the number of grams in 1 mol of a substance, so its unit is g/mol. For water it is 18.015 g/mol: 1 mol of H2O molecules has a mass of 18.015 g.

prompt: One molecule of caffeine has a mass of 194.19 u. What is the mass of 1 mol of caffeine molecules?

choices.why: That is the mass of one molecule. A mole contains 6.022 × 10^23 molecules, and its mass is given in grams.
This multiplies one molecule's mass by the number of molecules but labels the total in grams instead of u. Expressed in grams, 6.022 × 10^23 molecules of 194.19 u each have a mass of just 194.19 g.
That is the mass of a single caffeine molecule expressed in grams, not the mass of a whole mole.

explanation: A mole of a substance has the same mass in grams as one of its molecules has in atomic mass units. So 1 mol of caffeine has a mass of 194.19 g.

prompt: Chlorine gas is made of Cl2 molecules, and the atomic mass of chlorine is 35.453 u. A student says that 1.00 mol of chlorine gas has a mass of 35.453 g. What is wrong with this claim?

choices.text: Each Cl2 molecule has two atoms, so 1.00 mol of chlorine gas has a mass of 70.906 g.
Each Cl2 molecule has two atoms, so 1.00 mol of chlorine gas has a mass of 17.73 g.
choices.why: A molecule of two atoms is heavier than one atom, not lighter. The mass doubles; it isn't halved.

choices.text: The mass of 1.00 mol should be given in atomic mass units: 35.453 u.
choices.why: A mass in u describes one atom or molecule. The mass of a whole mole is given in grams.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong: 35.453 g is the mass of 1.00 mol of chlorine in any form.
choices.why: 35.453 g is the mass of 1 mol of chlorine atoms. Chlorine gas consists of Cl2 molecules, each twice as heavy as one atom.

explanation: One Cl2 molecule has a mass of 2 × 35.453 u = 70.906 u, so 1.00 mol of Cl2 molecules has a mass of 70.906 g. The student's 35.453 g is the mass of 1 mol of chlorine atoms.

prompt: You know how many molecules of ammonia, NH3, are in a sample and want to find the number of moles. Which conversion factor should you multiply by?

choices.text: 1 mol NH3 / 6.022 × 10^23 molecules NH3
6.022 × 10^23 molecules NH3 / 1 mol NH3
choices.why: This factor is upside down: the molecule units wouldn't cancel, and the answer would come out enormously too large.

choices.text: 17.03 g NH3 / 1 mol NH3
choices.why: The molar mass converts between moles and grams, not between moles and a number of molecules.

choices.text: 1 mol NH3 / 17.03 g NH3
choices.why: This factor converts a mass in grams into moles. You are starting from a number of molecules, not a mass.

explanation: The definition of a mole gives the equality 1 mol = 6.022 × 10^23 molecules. To cancel molecules and introduce moles, put molecules on the bottom: 1 mol / 6.022 × 10^23 molecules.

prompt: How many atoms are in 0.25 mol of copper? (Copper's molar mass is 63.546 g/mol.)

choices.why: This divides Avogadro's number by 0.25 instead of multiplying. A quarter of a mole must be fewer atoms than a whole mole.
This divides 0.25 by Avogadro's number, which gives less than one atom. Moles are converted to atoms by multiplying by 6.022 × 10^23.

choices.text: 15.9 atoms
choices.why: This multiplies by the molar mass, which gives the sample's mass in grams, 15.9 g, not its number of atoms.

explanation: Multiply the moles by Avogadro's number: 0.25 mol × 6.022 × 10^23 atoms/mol = 1.5 × 10^23 atoms. The molar mass isn't needed to count atoms.

prompt: A single grain of table salt contains about 1.0 × 10^−6 mol of NaCl. About how many NaCl units does the grain contain?
explanation: Multiply by Avogadro's number: 1.0 × 10^−6 mol × 6.022 × 10^23 units/mol = 6.0 × 10^17 NaCl units. Even a millionth of a mole is an enormous number of particles.

prompt: A party balloon is filled with about 3.5 × 10^23 helium atoms. How many moles of helium is that?
explanation: Divide by Avogadro's number: 3.5 × 10^23 atoms × (1 mol / 6.022 × 10^23 atoms) = 0.58 mol He.

prompt: Rust is mostly iron(III) oxide, Fe2O3. How many moles of oxygen atoms are in 2.50 mol of Fe2O3?
explanation: Each Fe2O3 unit contains 3 O atoms, so each mole of Fe2O3 contains 3 mol of O atoms: 2.50 mol × 3 = 7.50 mol of O atoms.

prompt: A sample of propane, C3H8, contains 2.40 × 10^24 hydrogen atoms. How many moles of propane are in the sample?
explanation: Moles of H atoms: 2.40 × 10^24 ÷ 6.022 × 10^23 = 3.985 mol. Each C3H8 molecule has 8 H atoms, so the sample holds 3.985 mol ÷ 8 = 0.498 mol of propane.

prompt: Suppose a machine could count atoms at a rate of one billion (10^9) atoms every second, nonstop. About how many years would it take to count 1 mol of atoms? (1 year = 3.16 × 10^7 s.)
explanation: 6.022 × 10^23 atoms ÷ 10^9 atoms/s = 6.022 × 10^14 s. Then 6.022 × 10^14 s ÷ 3.16 × 10^7 s/year = 1.91 × 10^7 years, about 19 million years.

prompt: What is the molar mass of aluminum sulfate, Al2(SO4)3, in g/mol? (Atomic masses: Al, 26.982 u; S, 32.065 u; O, 15.999 u.)
explanation: The parentheses mean three sulfate groups, so the formula has 2 Al, 3 S and 12 O: 2 × 26.982 + 3 × 32.065 + 12 × 15.999 = 53.964 + 96.195 + 191.988 = 342.147 g/mol.

prompt: A chemist finds that 0.250 mol of an unknown gas has a mass of 11.0 g. What is the molar mass of the gas, in g/mol?
explanation: Molar mass is grams per mole: 11.0 g ÷ 0.250 mol = 44.0 g/mol.

prompt: A student wants the number of moles in 50.0 g of water, H2O (molar mass 18.015 g/mol), and writes: 50.0 g × (18.015 g / 1 mol) = 901 mol. What is the mistake?

choices.text: The molar mass is upside down; using 1 mol / 18.015 g gives 2.78 mol.
The molar mass should be 18.015 u, since it is the mass of one molecule.
choices.why: 18.015 u is the mass of one molecule. Converting grams to moles needs the mass of a whole mole, 18.015 g.

choices.text: Avogadro's number is also needed, since moles are counted in molecules.
choices.why: Avogadro's number is needed only to get a number of molecules. Going from grams to moles uses the molar mass alone.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong: 50.0 g of water really is about 901 mol.
choices.why: One mole of water is 18.015 g, so 50.0 g is less than 3 mol. In the student's setup the gram units don't cancel.

explanation: To cancel grams and introduce moles, grams must be on the bottom of the factor: 50.0 g × (1 mol / 18.015 g) = 2.78 mol. Checking the units catches the error: g × g/mol does not give mol.

prompt: Which sample has the greater mass: 0.500 mol of carbon dioxide, CO2, or 1.00 mol of water, H2O? (Molar masses: CO2, 44.01 g/mol; H2O, 18.015 g/mol.)

choices.text: The CO2: 22.0 g, compared with 18.0 g of water
The water: it has twice as many moles as the CO2
choices.why: More moles means more molecules, but each CO2 molecule is much heavier. 0.500 mol × 44.01 g/mol = 22.0 g, more than the water's 18.0 g.

choices.text: The water: 18.0 g, compared with 0.0114 g of CO2
choices.why: 0.0114 comes from dividing 0.500 by 44.01. To get grams from moles, multiply by the molar mass: 0.500 mol × 44.01 g/mol = 22.0 g.

choices.text: The water: it contains more atoms than the CO2
choices.why: It does contain more atoms, 3.00 mol versus 1.50 mol, but carbon and oxygen atoms are much heavier than hydrogen atoms, so the CO2 has the greater mass.

explanation: Convert each amount to grams with its molar mass. CO2: 0.500 mol × 44.01 g/mol = 22.0 g. Water: 1.00 mol × 18.015 g/mol = 18.0 g. Fewer moles can still weigh more when each molecule is heavier.

prompt: An empty aluminum soda can has a mass of 14.5 g. Treating the can as pure aluminum, how many moles of aluminum atoms does it contain? (Molar mass of Al: 26.982 g/mol.)
explanation: Use the molar mass with grams on the bottom: 14.5 g Al × (1 mol Al / 26.982 g Al) = 0.537 mol Al.

prompt: A science demonstration calls for 0.0450 mol of baking soda, NaHCO3, which has a molar mass of 84.01 g/mol. What mass of baking soda, in grams, should you weigh out?
explanation: Use the molar mass with grams on top: 0.0450 mol × (84.01 g / 1 mol) = 3.78 g of NaHCO3.

prompt: Natural chalk is made of calcium carbonate, CaCO3. Treating a 12.5 g piece of chalk as pure CaCO3, how many moles of CaCO3 does it contain? (Atomic masses: Ca, 40.078 u; C, 12.011 u; O, 15.999 u.)
explanation: First the molar mass: 40.078 + 12.011 + 3 × 15.999 = 100.086 g/mol. Then 12.5 g × (1 mol / 100.086 g) = 0.125 mol of CaCO3.

prompt: A piece of aluminum foil and a gold coin each have a mass of 10.0 g. How many times as many atoms does the aluminum foil contain as the gold coin? (Molar masses: Al, 26.982 g/mol; Au, 196.97 g/mol.)
explanation: Aluminum: 10.0 g ÷ 26.982 g/mol = 0.371 mol. Gold: 10.0 g ÷ 196.97 g/mol = 0.0508 mol. The ratio is 0.371 ÷ 0.0508 = 7.30, the same as 196.97 ÷ 26.982: lighter atoms mean more of them in the same mass.

prompt: You know the number of atoms in a piece of silver and want its mass in grams. Silver's molar mass is 107.87 g/mol. Which single conversion factor does this in one step?

choices.why: This factor is upside down. Atoms must be on the bottom to cancel the atoms you start with.

choices.text: 107.87 g Ag / 1 atom Ag
choices.why: 107.87 g is the mass of a whole mole of silver atoms, not of a single atom.

choices.text: 107.87 g Ag / 1 mol Ag
choices.why: This converts moles, not atoms, into grams. Multiplying a number of atoms by it gives a mass 6.022 × 10^23 times too large.

explanation: One mole of silver is both 107.87 g and 6.022 × 10^23 atoms, so 107.87 g Ag = 6.022 × 10^23 atoms Ag. To cancel atoms and introduce grams, put grams on top: 107.87 g Ag / 6.022 × 10^23 atoms Ag.

prompt: A drop of water from an eyedropper has a mass of 0.0500 g. How many water molecules are in the drop? (Molar mass of H2O: 18.015 g/mol.)
explanation: Moles: 0.0500 g ÷ 18.015 g/mol = 2.78 × 10^−3 mol. Molecules: 2.78 × 10^−3 mol × 6.022 × 10^23 molecules/mol = 1.67 × 10^21 molecules.

prompt: A sugar cube contains 2.30 g of sucrose, C12H22O11, whose molar mass is 342.29 g/mol. How many carbon atoms are in the sugar cube?
explanation: Moles of sucrose: 2.30 g ÷ 342.29 g/mol = 6.72 × 10^−3 mol. Each molecule has 12 C atoms, so the number of carbon atoms is 6.72 × 10^−3 mol × 12 × 6.022 × 10^23 = 4.86 × 10^22.

prompt: A small crystal of aspirin, C9H8O4, contains 2.00 × 10^20 molecules. What is the mass of the crystal, in grams? (Molar mass of aspirin: 180.16 g/mol.)
What is the mass, in grams, of a single gold atom? (Molar mass of Au: 196.97 g/mol.)
explanation: One mole of gold atoms, 6.022 × 10^23 of them, has a mass of 196.97 g, so one atom has a mass of 196.97 g ÷ 6.022 × 10^23 = 3.27 × 10^−22 g.

prompt: A procedure calls for 0.150 mol of acetone, C3H6O, a liquid with a density of 0.785 g/mL and a molar mass of 58.08 g/mol. What volume of acetone, in mL, should you measure out?
explanation: Mass needed: 0.150 mol × 58.08 g/mol = 8.71 g. Volume: 8.71 g ÷ 0.785 g/mL = 11.1 mL.

prompt: Liquid mercury has a density of 13.5 g/mL and a molar mass of 200.59 g/mol. How many mercury atoms are in 1.00 mL of mercury?
